extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents/applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and overcoming pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections (novelty, public use, on-sale, printed publications) including affidavit/declaration practice, timing rules, and effective filing date issues (including CIPs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaiming affidavits to remove co-authored publication as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the inventor or at least one joint inventor is one of the co-authors of a publication cited against the application, the publication may be removed as a reference by the filing of affidavits made out by the other authors establishing that the relevant portions of the publication originated with, or were obtained from, the inventor or at least one joint inventor (called disclaiming affidavits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such affidavits (Ex parte Hirschler) or a specific declaration by the inventor showing the article describes the inventor's own work (In re Katz) may overcome the rejection. If a co-author refuses to disclaim inventorship and provides contrary evidence, the inventor's affidavit/declaration will not be enough (Ex parte Kroger). It is also possible to add coauthors as joint inventors if the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 116, third paragraph, are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 37 CFR 1.131 and 1.132 affidavits to antedate or show derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the reference is not a statutory bar under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b), applicant can overcome the rejection by swearing back of the reference through the submission of an affidavit under 37 CFR 1.131. If the reference is disclosing the inventor's or at least one joint inventor's own work as derived from the inventor or joint inventor, either a 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit to antedate the reference or a 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit to show derivation may be submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Foster and In re Facius for precedents, and MPEP § 715 for details on when a 1.131 affidavit can be used and what evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naked assertion of inventorship is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 that is only a naked assertion of inventorship and that fails to provide any context, explanation or evidence to support that assertion is insufficient to show that the relied-upon subject matter was the inventor’s own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EmeraChem Holdings v. Volkswagen found that a bare declaration without context, explanation, or evidence was insufficient, especially where many years had passed; declarations must provide supporting facts and evidence to lend credence to inventorship assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1-year grace period extension for holidays/weekends
rubrics_metrics.description: Publications, patents, public uses and sales must occur 'more than one year prior to the date of application for patent in the United States' to bar a patent under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b). However, the 1-year grace period is extended to the next business day if it would otherwise end on a Saturday, Sunday, or federal holiday (35 U.S.C. 21(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 35 U.S.C. 21(b) extension applies notwithstanding rules that accord filing dates by deposit or electronic submission (37 CFR 1.6, 1.10, 1.6(a)(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: 1-year time bar measured from the U.S. filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The 1-year time bar is measured from the U.S. filing date. Applicant will be barred from obtaining a patent if the public came into possession of the invention on a date before the 1-year grace period ending with the U.S. filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It does not matter how the public came into possession (public use, sale, publication, patent). Prior art need not be identical but will bar patentability if it is an obvious variant (In re Katz; In re Foster). See MPEP § 2139.01 regarding effective U.S. filing date issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective filing date for CIP claims determined claim-by-claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date of a claimed invention is determined on a claim-by-claim basis and not an application-by-application basis in continuation-in-part (CIP) situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any claim that is fully supported in the parent application has the parent's effective filing date; any claim that contains limitations only supported by the CIP has the CIP filing date. Prior art with a critical date more than one year prior to the child filing date will bar claims that have the child filing date (e.g., Paperless Accounting v. BART; Santarus; Studiengesellschaft Kohle v. Shell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's own pre-grace-period disclosures are prior art under 102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any invention described in a printed publication more than one year prior to the date of a patent application is prior art under Section 102(b), even if the printed publication was authored by the patent applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (De Graffenried; Bonito Boats) stresses that once an inventor publicly discloses the invention outside of the patent system, the choice is between seeking federal patent protection or dedicating the idea to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: 102(b) rejection creates a statutory bar that cannot be overcome by affidavits/priority/evidence of prior invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) cannot be overcome by affidavits and declarations under 37 CFR 1.131 (Rule 131 declarations), foreign priority dates, or evidence that applicant himself invented the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside the 1-year grace period, applicant is barred from obtaining a patent containing any anticipated or obvious claims (In re Foster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible ways to overcome a pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection based on pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) can be overcome by: (A) persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) submitting and perfecting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 within the time period set in 37 CFR 1.78 (or filing a petition under 1.78), and establishing that the prior application satisfies enablement/written description requirements; or (D) submitting and perfecting a benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) (or filing a grantable petition under 1.78).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For (C) applicants filed on/after 9/16/2012 should file a corrected ADS under 37 CFR 1.76 referring to the prior application; pre-9/16/2012 applicants may amend the specification or file a corrected ADS. Establishment of benefit requires meeting enablement and written description per 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112 first paragraph). PLTIA (effective 12/18/2013) may allow restoration of provisional benefit in some circumstances (see MPEP §§211, 211.01(a)). If the prior art qualifies under 102(a) after benefit perfection, see MPEP § 2132.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use test: accessible to the public or commercially exploited
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper test for the public use prong of pre-AIA §102(b) is whether the purported use: (1) was accessible to the public; or (2) was commercially exploited. Commercial exploitation is a clear indication of public use, but it likely requires more than, for example, a secret offer for sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test includes consideration of evidence relevant to experimentation, the nature of the activity that occurred in public, public access to the use, confidentiality obligations imposed on observers, and commercial exploitation. This evidence is relevant to whether the use was a public use but is distinct from the 'ready for patenting' component of Pfaff's two-part on-sale/public-use test (Invitrogen v. Biocrest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public knowledge is not necessarily public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere knowledge of the invention by the public does not warrant rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b); 102(b) bars public use or sale, not public knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although public knowledge may provide grounds under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), it is not alone sufficient for a 102(b) public-use rejection (TP Labs. v. Professional Positioners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial versus noncommercial use and the impact of secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret or confidential use alone is not sufficient to show that knowledge has not been withdrawn from public use; commercial exploitation is also forbidden. Secret internal commercial use may still create a public use bar if it represents commercial exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invitrogen: secret internal use to develop future products that were never sold was by itself insufficient to create a public use bar. The distinction between commercial and noncommercial contexts and how 'experimental use' is treated depends on the facts (see MPEP §2133.03(c) and subsections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-secret use is not ipso facto public use (and vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Public use' and 'non-secret use' are not necessarily synonymous; the fact that non-secret uses were made prior to the critical date is not itself dispositive of whether activity barring a patent occurred, nor is all secret use necessarily not public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider totality and policies underlying public use/on-sale bars; both secrecy and other circumstances (commercial exploitation, control by inventor) must be analyzed (TP Labs.; Moleculon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Display or hidden component in larger machine can constitute public use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor or someone connected to the inventor puts an invention on display or sells it in a larger machine or article that is accessible to the public, there is a public use even though the inventive component may be hidden from view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (In re Blaisdell; Ex parte Kuklo; Hall v. Macneale) show that use in its natural and intended way accessible to visitors can be public use even if inner workings were not visible; observers need not understand the technical significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private personal use does not create public use
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's private use of the invention for his or her own enjoyment is not a public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: inventor showing a puzzle to close friends in a private dorm room was not a public use because the inventor retained control (Moleculon Research Corp. v. CBS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of confidentiality agreement is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence or absence of a confidentiality agreement is not determinative of the public use issue, but is one factor to consider in assessing the totality of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasize analyzing all circumstances against the policies underlying the public use/on-sale bars (Bernhardt v. Collezione Europa). Consider nature of activity, public access, and confidentiality obligations; e.g., restricted invitation-only exhibitions with escorts may still require further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use occurs when inventor allows another to use invention without restriction or secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA public use occurs when the inventor allows another to use the invention without limitation, restriction or obligation of secrecy to the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Smith and related cases highlight that absence of restrictions/confidentiality and the amount of control retained by the inventor are key; sales or contracts permitting others to use commercially (Ex parte C) can create public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by independent third parties can be public use if it 'informs' the public or is ascertainable
rubrics_metrics.description: Any nonsecret use of an invention by an unrelated third party in the ordinary course of business may be a public use if it sufficiently informs the public of the invention or if a competitor could reasonably ascertain the invention (e.g., by inspection or analysis of sold/displayed products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventive details are ascertainable from the product sold or displayed, even a secret use can be public (Gillman; Dunlop). If third party maintained trade secrecy and details are not ascertainable, then the use may not be public (W.L. Gore). A device may still qualify as prior art if it placed claimed features in the public's possession even if other aspects remained confidential (Lockwood). Consider factual circumstances and policies underlying the bars; if not informing, other statutes like 102(f) or 102(g) may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar: impermissible sale or offer more than one year before effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: An impermissible sale has occurred if there was a definite sale, or offer to sell, more than one year before the effective filing date of the claimed invention and the subject matter of the sale or offer fully anticipated the claimed invention or would have rendered the claimed invention obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ferag AG v. Quipp and other cases demonstrate that a sale/offer more than one year prior can trigger the on-sale bar if it anticipates or combines to make the claim obvious. The on-sale bar can operate alone or in conjunction with 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pfaff two-part test for on-sale bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The on-sale bar of pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b) is triggered if the invention is both (1) the subject of a commercial offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes and (2) ready for patenting (Pfaff v. Wells Electronics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traditional contract law (UCC principles) is applied to determine whether a commercial offer for sale occurred (Linear Tech; Group One). Whether an offer constitutes a sale depends on concrete offer and acceptance; order acknowledgements or conditional language may indicate no accepted sale (e.g., 'will advise-not booked').

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'sale' under UCC and passage of title as indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'on sale' under §102(b), a product must be the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale, and to be a commercial sale it must bear the general hallmarks of a sale pursuant to the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC). Section 2-106 describes a 'sale' as 'the passing of title from the seller to the buyer for a price.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage of title is a helpful indicator of whether a product is 'on sale' (Medicines Co. v. Hospira). Courts will look to UCC §2-106 and related contract law to decide whether communications rise to the level of a commercial offer for sale.
